clue.text: Letters somewhere in South Africa after delivery

parts.note: letters arriving by mail are the post
Natal is a former province of South Africa, now KwaZulu-Natal

explanation.surface: A request for mail to be sent on to some place in South Africa once a delivery has gone out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delivery' reads as the postman's round, but here it means childbirth.
explanation.definitionFit: Postnatal describes the period following childbirth, which is a delivery of a baby.

clue.text: Girl taken in by political leader's religious air

indicators.note: being taken in by something means being held inside it, so the girl's name sits within the leader

parts.note: PM is the Prime Minister, the head of a British government
Sal is a short form of the girl's name Sally

explanation.surface: A young woman is won over by a politician's pious manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Air' looks like a manner or bearing, but it is a tune.
explanation.definitionFit: A psalm is a sacred song or hymn, so a religious tune.

clue.text: Father penning controversial novel with no leading character — as a game

indicators.note: penning means enclosing, as in a pen, so the novel goes inside the father

parts.note: to sire is to father, and a sire is a male parent

indicators.note: the novel's first letter is dropped, its leading character in the sense of initial letter

parts.note: Lolita, Nabokov's novel, caused a scandal on publication

explanation.surface: A dad writing a scandalous book without a main protagonist, treating it as a pastime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading character' suggests a novel's hero, but here it means the book title's first letter, which 'with no leading character' drops; 'penning' puts what is left inside the father.
explanation.definitionFit: Solitaire is a card game or peg game played by one person.

clue.text: Entrant not running -or entrants running

indicators.note: running here means in a liquid, flowing state, so the letters of the two words flow into a new order

explanation.surface: A race card note about a horse that has been withdrawn while the rest set off.
explanation.walkthrough: The same word 'running' serves twice in the surface, once in its race sense in the definition and once as the anagram signal on OR ENTRANTS.
explanation.definitionFit: A non-starter is a horse or competitor entered for a race that does not take part.

clue.text: Paddy has so much French spirit

parts.note: tant is French for so much
rum is a spirit distilled from sugar cane

explanation.surface: An Irishman drinks a great deal of brandy or the like.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paddy' looks like a name for an Irishman, but it is the British informal word for a fit of temper.
explanation.definitionFit: In British English a paddy is a fit of temper, which is a tantrum.

clue.text: Convict and non-U jailer in trailer

parts.note: an old lag is British slang for a convict

indicators.note: non-U means without the letter U, playing on the British idea of non-U, not upper-class

parts.note: a guard keeps prisoners in jail

explanation.surface: A prisoner and a common warder are inside a caravan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Non-U' is a British term for not upper-class speech or manners; here it simply removes the U from GUARD. 'Trailer' looks like a vehicle but means one who trails behind.
explanation.definitionFit: A laggard is someone who falls behind others, which is a trailer.

clue.text: West Country female

parts.note: Oman is a country on the Arabian peninsula

explanation.surface: A girl from the West Country, the south-western counties of England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'West Country' reads as one name for south-west England but splits into W and a country.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman is an adult female person.

clue.text: Inventor would arrange test tubes for starters

indicators.note: for starters means taking the opening letter of each of the following words

explanation.surface: A scientist who would set out some test tubes in the lab.
explanation.walkthrough: James WATT was the Scottish engineer who improved the steam engine.
explanation.definitionFit: James Watt was an engineer famed as an inventor, notably of a better steam engine.

clue.text: Island has whisky and soda finally

parts.note: malt is a whisky made from malted barley

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word soda

explanation.surface: An island where the drink is whisky with soda.
explanation.definitionFit: Malta is a Mediterranean island nation south of Sicily.

clue.text: Piece of cake thrown in or near bin

indicators.note: thrown in suggests tossing things in a jumble, so the letters are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: A slice of cake tossed into the rubbish, or close to the bin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thrown in' looks like it goes with 'Piece of cake', but it is the anagram signal on OR NEAR BIN.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-brainer is something so easy it needs no thought, like a piece of cake.

clue.text: Exhausted subset of structural linguistics

indicators.note: a subset is a part taken from a set, so a run of letters is lifted out of these words

explanation.surface: Worn out by a branch of linguistic study.
explanation.definitionFit: All in is an informal phrase meaning completely tired.

clue.text: Place of entertainment near Bath overwhelming couple from Clifton

parts.note: nigh is an old word for near

indicators.note: overwhelming means covering or engulfing, so the bath surrounds the letters from Clifton

parts.note: a tub is a bath

indicators.note: a couple from means the first two letters of the word Clifton

explanation.surface: A venue near the city of Bath swamping a pair of people from Clifton, a district of Bristol.
explanation.walkthrough: Bath and Clifton are real places in the west of England, but 'Bath' here is a tub, and CL goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A nightclub is a venue open late for dancing and entertainment.

clue.text: Meat cooked by sailor — and another wanting T bone

indicators.note: cooked means altered or prepared, so the letters of meat are rearranged

parts.note: a tar is a sailor

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so the letter T is removed

parts.note: another sailor: an old salt is a seasoned sailor

explanation.surface: Meat prepared by a sailor and his mate, minus a T-bone steak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooked' makes META from MEAT; 'another' means another sailor, SALT, which 'wanting T' cuts to SAL. 'T bone' looks like a steak, but 'bone' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A metatarsal is one of the long bones of the foot.

clue.text: What doll may say in Outer Mongolia repeatedly

indicators.note: repeatedly means the pair of letters is given twice over
outer means the outside letters of the word Mongolia, its first and last

explanation.surface: A talking doll that cries out a word over and over in remote Mongolia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outer Mongolia' looks like a place name, but 'Outer' takes the M and A at the ends of MONGOLIA.
explanation.definitionFit: Talking dolls traditionally say the childish word for mother.

clue.text: How statement may be used is to be seen

definitions.meaning: a police caution warns that what you say may be given in court as part of the case
visible, noticeable, present to the eye

explanation.walkthrough: The British police caution says anything you say may be given in evidence.
explanation.definitionFit: A statement is used as part of the case in court, and the phrase also means plainly visible.

clue.text: Clutching one penny, Mrs Simpson comes back with witty remark

indicators.note: comes back means the whole assembled piece is read in the opposite direction
clutching means holding, so the cartoon wife grips the two letters inside her

parts.note: Marge Simpson is the mother in the cartoon series The Simpsons
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Marge Simpson returns holding a coin and makes a clever quip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mrs Simpson' suggests Wallis Simpson, but it is Marge; IP goes in MARGE after the G and 'comes back' turns the lot.
explanation.definitionFit: An epigram is a short, clever and pithy saying.

clue.text: Dawn raider not getting back — roughly 100 years old?

indicators.note: roughly means approximately or carelessly, so the letters are put in a rough new order
not getting the back means losing the last letter of raider

explanation.surface: A thief at daybreak who fails to return, a century ago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not getting back' drops the final letter of the second word; 'roughly' shuffles what remains. The question mark flags a loose definition: Edward VII's reign was about a century before this 2010 puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: The Edwardian period, 1901 to 1910, was roughly a century old when the puzzle was set.

clue.text: To perform with star, name is required -Mellow Yellow Fellow?

parts.note: to do is to perform
a nova is a star that suddenly brightens

explanation.surface: Joining a celebrity on stage needs a name, says the man behind a hit song.
explanation.walkthrough: Mellow Yellow was a 1966 hit for the Scottish singer DONOVAN; the rhyming 'Fellow' and the question mark point to the singer.
explanation.definitionFit: The singer Donovan recorded the song Mellow Yellow, so he is that song's man.

clue.text: Country location in which Emile Zola started French article

indicators.note: in which means the letters are put inside the location

parts.note: a venue is the location of an event

indicators.note: started points to the opening letters of the two names Emile and Zola

parts.note: la is the feminine definite article in French

explanation.surface: A place where the novelist Emile Zola began a newspaper piece in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' suggests a piece of writing, but it is the grammatical article; 'in which' puts the novelist's initials inside the location.
explanation.definitionFit: Venezuela is a country on the north coast of South America.

clue.text: Small boy going to Land's End for a couple of days

parts.note: wee is Scottish for small
Ken is a boy's name

indicators.note: end points to the closing letter of the word land

explanation.surface: A little lad travelling to Land's End, the tip of Cornwall, for a short break.
explanation.walkthrough: Land's End is the far western tip of England in Cornwall; here 'End' takes the D from LAND.
explanation.definitionFit: A weekend is Saturday and Sunday, two days.

clue.text: Ruddy dog's first to have caught vermin

indicators.note: first means the opening letter of the word dog

parts.note: to rat is to hunt rats, so having caught vermin is having ratted

explanation.surface: A red-coated terrier has to have killed some rats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruddy' looks like a colour, but it is a mild British oath, like 'blooming'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruddy and dratted are both mild British expletives meaning confounded.

clue.text: One may find water in heavenly river

parts.note: divine means heavenly

explanation.surface: Someone discovers water in a celestial stream.
explanation.walkthrough: A diviner (dowser) searches for underground water with a rod.
explanation.definitionFit: A diviner, or dowser, locates underground water with a forked stick.

clue.text: Champions fed up with tips

indicators.note: up in a down clue means read upwards, so the word fed is reversed

parts.note: the tips of things are their ends

explanation.surface: Winners who have had enough of advice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Champions' looks like a plural noun, but it is the verb: to champion is to defend.
explanation.definitionFit: To champion a cause is to support or protect it, which is to defend it.

clue.text: Legal documents reported ostentatious luxury

indicators.note: reported means spoken, so the letters entered match the sound of the legal word

parts.note: writs are formal legal orders

explanation.surface: Court papers give an account of showy extravagance.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ritz is a famously grand London hotel, hence 'putting on the Ritz' for showy luxury.
explanation.definitionFit: Named for the grand hotels, ritz is informal for flashy, showy luxury.

clue.text: Hooker seen in street alone

indicators.note: seen in means the run of letters is visible inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A prostitute spotted on the street by herself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hooker' looks like a prostitute, but it means something with a hook, a claw.
explanation.definitionFit: A talon is a hooked claw, so a thing that hooks prey.

clue.text: Prince of Zenda getting complex number

parts.note: Prince Hal is the young Henry V in Shakespeare's history plays

indicators.note: complex means tangled or intricate, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: The Prisoner of Zenda hero acquires a psychological complex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prince of Zenda' suggests the Ruritanian novel, but Prince is HAL and OF ZENDA is anagrammed.
explanation.definitionFit: Half a dozen is six, a number.

clue.text: Girl's beginning to enter with no clothes on -that's to attract attention

definitions.note: the defining words describe a noun, a gentle push given for a purpose

indicators.note: to enter means the letter goes inside the naked word

parts.note: nude means wearing no clothes

indicators.note: beginning points to the first letter of the word girl

explanation.surface: A young woman starts going about naked to get noticed.
explanation.definitionFit: A nudge is a light push with the elbow given to draw someone's notice.

clue.text: Just working fifty years

parts.note: on means working, as of a machine switched on
L is the Roman numeral fifty

explanation.surface: Merely being employed for half a century.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just' looks like fair, but it means merely.
explanation.definitionFit: Only and just both mean merely or no more than.

clue.text: Incredible claim of one throwing weight about somewhere in London?

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
to sling is to throw
a ton is a weight

explanation.surface: A strongman's boast that he can hurl a heavy load, wherever he happens to be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Incredible claim of' and 'about' frame the boast 'I sling ton' as a hurler might make it. Islington is a London borough.
explanation.definitionFit: Islington is a borough of north London, so a place in the capital.

clue.text: Donne composed a lot

indicators.note: composed means made up or put together, so the poet's letters are arranged afresh

explanation.surface: The poet John Donne wrote a great deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Composed' fits the poet writing verse, but it signals the anagram of DONNE.
explanation.definitionFit: No end is an informal phrase meaning a great deal or very much.

clue.text: Silly Billy-3 in US state

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held is 'Silly Billy-3 in US state (5)': the '3' gives no letters; N + IN + NY needs an N there, likely an OCR misread of 'n', but no scan or online source confirms the printed text.

clue.text: Reckless squadron leader in repeated spin

indicators.note: in means the letter goes inside the word repeated
a spin is a whirl, so the letters are spun into a new order
leader points to the first letter of the word squadron

explanation.surface: A rash squadron leader caught in one aerial spin after another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Squadron leader' looks like an RAF rank, but it gives S, which goes in REPEATED before 'spin' shuffles the lot.
explanation.definitionFit: Desperate can mean reckless, acting rashly out of despair.
